attribution: Traditionally attributed to Patanjali; whether this Patanjali is the grammarian of the same name is debated
author: patanjali
period: Scholars commonly place the compilation between roughly the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE; many favour the early centuries CE
summary: The root text of the Yoga darshana: a terse manual on the mind, its afflictions, and the disciplined path to isolation of pure consciousness.
whyRead: It is the classical systematic account of yoga as a discipline of mind rather than of posture. Its short aphorisms define key terms that later Indian traditions, and modern yoga, keep returning to. Read it with a commentary; the sutras were written to be unpacked.
questions: What is the mind, and why is it restless?
Can the mind be brought to stillness, and what remains when it is still?
What are the practical steps from ethics to meditative absorption?

keyTeachings.title: Yoga as a discipline of the mind
keyTeachings.text: The text opens by defining yoga in terms of the mind-field (chitta) and its fluctuations (vritti). When these activities come to rest, the seer is said to abide in its own nature. Posture and breath serve this aim; they are not the goal.

keyTeachings.title: Practice and dispassion
keyTeachings.text: Steadiness is said to come from two complementary supports: sustained practice (abhyasa) and dispassion (vairagya) toward objects of experience. Commentators treat this pair as the backbone of the whole discipline.

keyTeachings.title: The five afflictions (kleshas)
keyTeachings.text: Suffering is traced to five afflictions: ignorance (avidya), I-am-ness (asmita), attraction, aversion and clinging to life. Ignorance, understood as mistaking the non-self for the self, is the ground of the other four.

keyTeachings.title: The eight limbs (ashtanga)
keyTeachings.text: The second and third chapters set out eight limbs: yama (ethical restraints), niyama (observances), asana (seated posture), pranayama (breath regulation), pratyahara (withdrawal of the senses), dharana (concentration), dhyana (meditation) and samadhi (absorption). The last three together are called samyama.

keyTeachings.title: Ishvara as a special purusha
keyTeachings.text: Unlike classical Sankhya, the Yoga Sutras admit Ishvara, a distinct purusha untouched by affliction and karma. Devotion or surrender to Ishvara (ishvara-pranidhana) is presented as one means to samadhi.

keyTeachings.title: Kaivalya: isolation of the seer
keyTeachings.text: The goal is kaivalya, the isolation of pure consciousness (purusha) from the workings of nature (prakriti). The text shares Sankhya's dualist framework while giving it a practical, meditative method.
